narrative:
The model determined that you have a 95.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for predicted success, this high risk of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were, in order: your class ranking in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average ranking of accepted students. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar. Your LSAT score of 26 was also well below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, adding further concern. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile—compared to an average around the sixth decile for those who were admitted—reinforced the same pattern of academic struggle.

Taken together, these performance signals made the model conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was simply too high to offer admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, seeking academic support to improve your class standing if you re-enroll, and perhaps exploring schools or programs with different admissions thresholds. Many students improve these metrics on a second attempt and go on to pass the bar successfully.
